label: Science, Tech, Awards & Sports
blurb: A comprehensive review of India's space and nuclear programmes, global awards, and major international sports tournaments.

topics.title: Chandrayaan-1: India's first lunar probe
topics.hook: Launched in 2008, Chandrayaan-1 discovered water molecules on the Moon.
topics.story:
Chandrayaan-1 was India's first lunar space probe, launching the ISRO Moon exploration program. It operated for 312 days and achieved 95% of its planned objectives. The mission carried 11 scientific instruments built in India, USA, UK, Germany, Sweden, and Bulgaria.

The most significant discovery was the widespread presence of water molecules in lunar soil, detected by the Moon Mineralogy Mapper instrument provided by NASA.
topics.why: CLAT will focus on the launch vehicle (PSLV-C11) and the specific instrument that discovered water (Moon Mineralogy Mapper).

topics.title: Chandrayaan-2: The partial success
topics.hook: Chandrayaan-2 aimed to land on the lunar south pole but the Vikram lander crashed during descent.
topics.story:
Launched in July 2019, Chandrayaan-2 comprised an orbiter, lander, and rover. The orbiter successfully entered lunar orbit and continues to map the surface.

The Vikram lander, carrying the Pragyan rover, deviated from its intended trajectory at an altitude of 2.1 kilometres and crashed. Despite the landing failure, the orbiter's scientific instruments provided high-resolution data.
topics.why: Examiners test the nomenclature—Vikram (named after Vikram Sarabhai) and Pragyan (wisdom)—and the launch vehicle.

topics.title: Chandrayaan-3: India lands on the lunar south pole
topics.hook: India became the first country to land a spacecraft near the lunar south pole in August 2023.
topics.story:
Chandrayaan-3 succeeded where its predecessor failed, achieving a soft landing near the lunar south pole on August 23, 2023. India became the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to land in the south polar region.

The mission consisted of a propulsion module, the Vikram lander, and the Pragyan rover. The south pole is strategically important due to the presence of water ice in permanently shadowed craters, which could support future human outposts.

The Pragyan rover conducted in-situ chemical analysis of the lunar surface, confirming the presence of sulphur and other elements. August 23 was subsequently declared National Space Day in India.
topics.why: Questions will target the specific names (Shiv Shakti Point), dates (August 23), and the elements confirmed by Pragyan (Sulphur).

topics.title: Aditya-L1: India's solar observatory
topics.hook: Aditya-L1 is India's first dedicated solar mission, placed in a halo orbit around Lagrange point 1.
topics.story:
Launched in September 2023, Aditya-L1 studies the solar atmosphere, specifically the chromosphere and corona. The spacecraft is positioned at Lagrange point 1 (L1) of the Sun-Earth system, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth.

The L1 point provides an uninterrupted view of the Sun without any eclipses. The primary instrument, the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), observes the solar corona and coronal mass ejections.
topics.why: CLAT tests the physics concept—what a Lagrange point is—and the specific payloads like VELC.

topics.title: Gaganyaan: India's human spaceflight programme
topics.hook: Gaganyaan aims to send a three-member crew to a low earth orbit and return them safely.
topics.story:
The Gaganyaan programme will demonstrate indigenous capability to undertake human spaceflight. ISRO plans to launch a crew of three to an orbit of 400 km for a three-day mission.

In February 2024, four astronaut designates—Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap, and Shubhanshu Shukla—were introduced to the public. They received training at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center in Russia.
topics.why: The names of the four astronauts and the specific orbit parameters (400 km LEO) are high-yield facts.

topics.title: Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)
topics.hook: India's first interplanetary mission made ISRO the fourth space agency to reach Mars.
topics.story:
The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), informally known as Mangalyaan, was launched in 2013 and entered Martian orbit in September 2014. India became the first Asian nation to reach Martian orbit and the first in the world to do so in its maiden attempt.

The mission was notable for its cost-effectiveness, costing roughly $74 million. It carried five scientific instruments to study the Martian surface features, morphology, mineralogy, and atmosphere.
topics.why: The achievement of first-attempt success and the specific year (2014 insertion) are the most tested angles.

topics.title: NASA Artemis Program: Return to the Moon
topics.hook: The Artemis program aims to establish a sustainable human presence on the Moon by the late 2020s.
topics.story:
Led by NASA, the Artemis program seeks to return humans to the Moon, including the first woman and the first person of colour. Artemis I, an uncrewed flight test of the Space Launch System (SLS) and Orion spacecraft, successfully launched in November 2022.

The program involves international partnerships through the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for space exploration. India signed the Artemis Accords in 2023.
topics.why: India's signing of the Artemis Accords is the primary geopolitical angle CLAT will test.

topics.title: James Webb Space Telescope
topics.hook: JWST is the largest and most powerful space telescope ever built, operating primarily in the infrared.
topics.story:
Launched in December 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is the scientific successor to the Hubble and Spitzer space telescopes. It orbits the Sun near the second Lagrange point (L2).

Its primary mirror consists of 18 hexagonal segments made of gold-plated beryllium. JWST's infrared capabilities allow it to see older, cooler, and more distant objects than Hubble.

topics.title: India's Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme
topics.hook: Formulated by Homi Bhabha, the program aims to utilize India's vast thorium reserves for energy independence.
topics.story:
Dr. Homi Bhabha conceived the three-stage nuclear power programme in the 1950s to secure India's long-term energy independence. The strategy is dictated by India's limited uranium reserves but abundant thorium reserves, found primarily in the monazite sands of Kerala.

Stage 1 uses Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) fueled by natural uranium to produce plutonium-239. Stage 2 uses Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) burning plutonium-239 to breed uranium-233 from thorium-232. Stage 3 uses Advanced Heavy Water Reactors (AHWRs) fueled by uranium-233 and thorium-232.

The 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam marks the transition to the second stage.
topics.why: Examiners frequently ask about the specific fuels for each stage and the location of the thorium reserves (Kerala).

topics.title: Pokhran-I: Smiling Buddha
topics.hook: India's first successful nuclear bomb test was conducted in 1974 under the code name Smiling Buddha.
topics.story:
On May 18, 1974, India conducted its first nuclear test at the Pokhran test range in Rajasthan. The operation, assigned the code name Smiling Buddha, was characterized by the Indian government as a 'peaceful nuclear explosion' (PNE).

The test made India the sixth country in the world to successfully detonate a nuclear device. It led to the formation of the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) by the international community to control nuclear exports.
topics.why: The code name 'Smiling Buddha' and the international reaction (formation of the NSG) are key takeaways.

topics.title: Pokhran-II: Operation Shakti
topics.hook: In May 1998, India conducted five nuclear tests, declaring itself a full-fledged nuclear weapon state.
topics.story:
Operation Shakti consisted of five nuclear bomb test explosions conducted at the Pokhran Test Range in May 1998. The tests included a thermonuclear device and fission devices.

Following the tests, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee officially declared India a nuclear weapons state. May 11 was subsequently designated as National Technology Day to commemorate the achievement.

topics.title: The Nobel Prizes: Categories and History
topics.hook: Established by Alfred Nobel's will, the prizes are awarded annually in six categories.
topics.story:
The Nobel Prizes were established by the 1895 will of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite. The prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, and Peace were first awarded in 1901.

In 1968, Sweden's central bank, Sveriges Riksbank, established the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. While not technically a Nobel Prize established by his will, it is administered and awarded alongside the others.

The Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, Norway, while the other five are awarded in Stockholm, Sweden. The maximum number of laureates per prize in a single year is three.
topics.why: The distinction of the Economics prize (established later by the central bank) and the Oslo location for the Peace Prize are classic traps.

topics.title: Indian Nobel Laureates
topics.hook: Rabindranath Tagore was the first Indian citizen to win a Nobel Prize, awarded for Literature in 1913.
topics.story:
Several Indian citizens and people of Indian origin have been awarded the Nobel Prize. Rabindranath Tagore became the first Asian laureate when he won the Literature prize in 1913 for 'Gitanjali'.

C.V. Raman won the Physics prize in 1930 for the discovery of the Raman Effect. Mother Teresa received the Peace Prize in 1979. Amartya Sen won the Economics prize in 1998 for his contributions to welfare economics. Kailash Satyarthi shared the Peace Prize in 2014 with Malala Yousafzai.

topics.title: Bharat Ratna: India's Highest Civilian Award
topics.hook: Instituted in 1954, the Bharat Ratna is awarded in recognition of exceptional service or performance of the highest order.
topics.story:
The Bharat Ratna was instituted on January 2, 1954. Originally limited to the arts, literature, science, and public services, the criteria were expanded in 2011 to include 'any field of human endeavour'.

The recommendations are made directly by the Prime Minister to the President. A maximum of three awards are typically granted in a single year, though exceptions have occurred (e.g., five in 2024). The first recipients were C. Rajagopalachari, Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, and C.V. Raman.
topics.why: The specific mechanism—that the PM recommends directly to the President without a formal committee—is a common constitutional trivia question.

topics.title: Padma Awards: Vibhushan, Bhushan, and Shri
topics.hook: Announced annually on Republic Day, the Padma Awards are the second, third, and fourth highest civilian honours.
topics.story:
The Padma Awards were instituted in 1954 alongside the Bharat Ratna. They are awarded in three categories: Padma Vibhushan (exceptional and distinguished service), Padma Bhushan (distinguished service of high order), and Padma Shri (distinguished service in any field).

The awards are conferred by the President of India at ceremonial functions held at Rashtrapati Bhavan, usually in March or April. The Padma Awards Committee, constituted by the Prime Minister every year, considers the nominations.

topics.title: The Modern Olympic Games
topics.hook: Inspired by the ancient Greek games, Pierre de Coubertin founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894.
topics.story:
The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, in 1896. Pierre de Coubertin is considered the father of the modern Olympics. He founded the International Olympic Committee (IOC), headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.

The Olympic motto is 'Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter' (Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together). The Olympic flag features five interlocking rings on a white background, representing the union of the five continents.

topics.title: Tennis Grand Slams: The Four Majors
topics.hook: The Grand Slam tournaments consist of the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open.
topics.story:
The four Grand Slam tournaments are the most important annual tennis events. Wimbledon, established in 1877, is the oldest and is played on grass. The US Open (1881) and Australian Open (1905) are played on hard courts. The French Open (1891), also known as Roland Garros, is played on clay.

Winning all four majors in a single calendar year is termed a 'Calendar Year Grand Slam'. Winning all four plus the Olympic gold medal is a 'Golden Slam', a feat achieved by Steffi Graf in 1988.

passages.title: ISRO's Lunar and Solar Triumphs
passages.passage:
In the span of a few weeks in late 2023, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) achieved two monumental milestones that cemented India's position as an elite spacefaring nation. The first was the successful soft landing of a spacecraft near the lunar south pole, a region of intense scientific interest due to the presence of permanently shadowed craters that may contain water ice. This achievement made India the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to reach the rugged southern terrain.

Shortly after, ISRO launched its maiden solar observatory, designed to study the solar atmosphere from a unique vantage point 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. This specific orbit, balancing the gravitational forces of the Earth and the Sun, allows the spacecraft to continuously view the Sun without any occultation or eclipses, providing real-time observation of solar activities and space weather.

These missions represent a significant leap in India's indigenous space capabilities. They involve complex orbital manoeuvres, advanced precision landing technologies, and sophisticated scientific payloads designed and developed entirely within the country. The data gathered from the lunar surface and the solar corona will contribute significantly to global scientific knowledge, answering fundamental questions about the evolution of the lunar surface and the dynamics of solar emissions.

questions.q: What is the primary scientific reason for targeting the lunar south pole?
options: It is the closest point to Earth.
It has a flatter terrain suitable for landing.
It contains permanently shadowed craters with potential water ice.
questions.explain: The passage explicitly states the south pole is of intense scientific interest 'due to the presence of permanently shadowed craters that may contain water ice'.

questions.q: What is the name of the gravitationally stable point where ISRO's solar observatory is placed?
questions.explain: Aditya-L1 is placed at Lagrange Point 1 (L1), 1.5 million km from Earth, allowing uninterrupted viewing of the Sun.

questions.q: Which launch vehicle was used for the lunar mission mentioned in the passage (Chandrayaan-3)?
questions.explain: Chandrayaan-3 was launched using the LVM3-M4 (Launch Vehicle Mark-III).

questions.q: What name was given to the landing site of the lunar mission near the south pole?
questions.explain: The landing site of Chandrayaan-3 was named Shiv Shakti Point by the Prime Minister.

questions.q: Which date is now celebrated as National Space Day in India to commemorate this lunar landing?
questions.explain: August 23 is celebrated as National Space Day to mark the successful landing of Chandrayaan-3.

passages.title: India's Nuclear Trajectory
passages.passage:
India's approach to nuclear technology has always been uniquely dictated by its domestic resource constraints and complex security environment. In the 1950s, anticipating the need for massive energy generation, a visionary physicist formulated a long-term strategy to bypass India's limited uranium reserves. This strategy relied instead on the country's vast coastal deposits of monazite sand, which contain a fertile material that can be converted into fissile fuel through a complex cycle of fast breeder and advanced heavy water reactors.

Simultaneously, India maintained a policy of strategic ambiguity regarding the military applications of nuclear technology. This ambiguity ended when India conducted its first underground nuclear test in the Rajasthan desert, characterizing it as a 'peaceful explosion'. The international reaction was swift, leading to the formation of a global export control cartel aimed at restricting India's access to nuclear commerce.

Two decades later, India definitively crossed the nuclear threshold with a series of five tests, officially declaring itself a nuclear weapons state. This dual trajectory—pursuing an intricate closed fuel cycle for energy while establishing a minimum credible nuclear deterrent—defines India's exceptional status in the global nuclear order today.

questions.q: Who formulated the long-term nuclear energy strategy mentioned in the first paragraph?
questions.explain: Dr. Homi Bhabha is the architect of India's three-stage nuclear power programme.

questions.q: What is the fertile material found in coastal monazite sands that India plans to use for stage three of its nuclear program?
questions.explain: India's long-term strategy relies on utilizing its vast Thorium reserves, found in monazite sands.

questions.q: What was the code name of the first underground nuclear test mentioned in the second paragraph?
questions.explain: The 1974 Pokhran-I test was code-named 'Smiling Buddha'.

questions.q: Which international export control cartel was formed in direct response to India's first nuclear test?
questions.explain: The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) was formed in 1974 to restrict nuclear exports following India's test.

questions.q: On which date were the subsequent five tests conducted, now celebrated as National Technology Day?
questions.explain: May 11 marks National Technology Day, commemorating the Pokhran-II tests (Operation Shakti) in 1998.

passages.title: The Legacy of Alfred Nobel
passages.passage:
When a wealthy Swedish industrialist and inventor drafted his last will and testament in 1895, he directed that the bulk of his fortune be used to establish a series of prizes. These awards were to be given to those who, during the preceding year, had conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. Originally, the prizes covered five specific fields: Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, and Peace.

Decades later, in 1968, a central bank celebrating its 300th anniversary established a sixth prize in Economic Sciences, funded by a donation to the foundation managing the original awards. While structurally identical in its selection process and prestige, it is officially distinct from the awards mandated by the 1895 will.

The administrative geography of the awards also reflects a historical nuance. While the scientific and literary prizes are handed out in the Swedish capital, the founder specified that the Peace Prize be awarded by a committee appointed by the parliament of a neighbouring country, which was in a political union with Sweden at the time the will was written. Several Indian citizens have been recognized across these categories, beginning with a literary giant in 1913.

questions.q: What invention made the founder of these prizes wealthy?
questions.explain: Alfred Nobel, the founder of the prizes, was the inventor of dynamite.

questions.q: Which institution established the prize in Economic Sciences in 1968?
questions.explain: Sveriges Riksbank established the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel in 1968.

questions.q: In which city is the Peace Prize awarded, as distinct from the other prizes?
questions.explain: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, Norway, while the others are awarded in Stockholm, Sweden.

questions.q: Who was the 'literary giant' from India who won the prize in 1913?
questions.explain: Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for 'Gitanjali'.

questions.q: According to the rules governing these awards, what is the maximum number of laureates who can share a single prize in a given year?
questions.explain: A maximum of three laureates can share a single Nobel Prize.

passages.title: Honouring Civilian Excellence in India
passages.passage:
In 1954, the Government of India instituted two overarching civilian awards to recognize exceptional contributions by individuals. The premier award is the highest civilian honour in the country, granted for exceptional service or performance of the highest order. Its criteria were expanded in 2011 from specific fields like art and science to encompass 'any field of human endeavour'. Uniquely, recommendations for this highest honour are made directly by the Prime Minister to the President, requiring no formal awards committee.

The second tier of awards is announced annually on the eve of Republic Day and comprises three classes, graded by the level of distinguished service. The selection process for these involves a committee constituted by the Prime Minister every year, which considers nominations from state governments, ministries, and citizens. 

While these awards confer immense prestige, they do not amount to titles, and Article 18 of the Constitution prohibits their use as prefixes or suffixes to the recipient's name. They represent the state's recognition of individuals who have enriched the nation through their exceptional talents and public service.

questions.q: What is the highest civilian honour in India, described in the first paragraph?
questions.explain: The Bharat Ratna is India's highest civilian award.

questions.q: Who recommends the names for the highest civilian honour directly to the President?
questions.explain: Recommendations for the Bharat Ratna are made directly by the Prime Minister to the President.

questions.q: Which of the following represents the correct hierarchical order of the second-tier civilian awards (from highest to lowest)?
options: Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Shri
Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri
Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan
Padma Vibhushan, Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan
questions.explain: The hierarchy is Padma Vibhushan (highest), followed by Padma Bhushan, and then Padma Shri.

questions.q: On which day are the Padma Awards annually announced?
questions.explain: The Padma Awards are announced annually on the eve of Republic Day (January 26).

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution prohibits the use of these civilian awards as titles (prefixes/suffixes)?
questions.explain: Article 18 of the Indian Constitution abolishes titles and prohibits using civilian awards as prefixes or suffixes.

passages.title: Pinnacles of Global Sport
passages.passage:
The landscape of international sports is defined by events that test the absolute limits of human endurance and skill. The most prominent multi-sport gathering traces its modern origins to 1896, when a French educator championed the revival of ancient athletic traditions. The governing body he established, now headquartered in Switzerland, manages an event that brings together nations under a flag featuring five interlocking rings. The ethos of this movement is encapsulated in a Latin motto urging athletes to be faster, higher, stronger—and, as updated recently, together.

In the realm of individual sports, tennis features four premier annual tournaments that constitute the pinnacle of achievement. These tournaments are characterized by their distinct playing surfaces, which demand vastly different styles of play. The oldest of these, held in London, is the only major still played on traditional grass courts. Another, held in Paris, tests players' stamina on slow clay courts. Winning all four within a single calendar year is a rare feat, defining a player's absolute dominance across all conditions.

questions.q: Who is considered the founder of the modern Olympic Games?
questions.explain: Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator, founded the IOC and revived the modern Olympics.

questions.q: Where is the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) located?
questions.explain: The IOC is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.

questions.q: What is the Latin motto of the Olympics, translated as 'Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together'?
questions.explain: The Olympic motto is 'Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter'.

questions.q: Which is the oldest tennis Grand Slam tournament, played on grass courts?
questions.explain: Wimbledon, established in 1877, is the oldest Grand Slam and the only one played on grass.

questions.q: Which Grand Slam tournament is played on clay courts in Paris?
questions.explain: The French Open, also known as Roland Garros, is played on clay courts in Paris.

passages.title: Global Team Championships
passages.passage:
Global team sports are governed by international federations that organise quadrennial or biennial world championships, generating massive global viewership. The premier international football tournament, inaugurated in 1930 and hosted by a South American nation, remains the most widely viewed sporting event globally. Its governing body, based in Switzerland, oversees a competition that has historically been dominated by a South American nation with five titles.

Similarly, the premier One Day International cricket tournament, first hosted in England in 1975, represents the pinnacle of the sport. The global governing body for cricket recently relocated its headquarters from London to the Middle East, reflecting the shifting economic center of gravity in the sport. India has claimed this title twice, marking significant milestones in its sporting history.

In badminton, international team supremacy is contested through two distinct gender-specific tournaments. The men's team championship was recently won by India for the first time in 2022 in a historic upset against a 14-time champion nation, highlighting India's rising prominence in global racquet sports.

questions.q: Which country hosted and won the inaugural FIFA World Cup in 1930?
questions.explain: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930.

questions.q: Where is the current headquarters of the International Cricket Council (ICC)?
questions.explain: The ICC relocated its headquarters from London to Dubai in 2005.

questions.q: In which years did India win the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup?
questions.explain: India won the ODI World Cup in 1983 (under Kapil Dev) and 2011 (under M.S. Dhoni).

questions.q: What is the name of the premier international men's team championship in badminton, which India won in 2022?
questions.explain: The Thomas Cup is the men's team championship in badminton; the Uber Cup is for women.

questions.q: Which country is the most successful in FIFA World Cup history with five titles?
questions.explain: Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup five times, the most of any nation.
